title: How to Get Perfect Lawn Stripes at Home
summary_html: Stripes are not painted on. They are light bending off bent grass. Here is how to get sharp, Wimbledon-style stripes with the right mower and the right technique.
seo_title: How to Get Perfect Lawn Stripes | MowDirect
seo_description: Get sharp, Wimbledon-style lawn stripes at home. How the rear roller works, mowing pattern, overlap and edges, plus the mowers that stripe best.
body_html:
You have seen it over the fence, or on the television during Wimbledon fortnight. A lawn cut into crisp light and dark bands, sharp enough to look painted on. It is not paint, and it is not a secret reserved for groundstaff. It is one piece of kit and a bit of method.

This guide explains how stripes actually form, the pattern to mow, and how to fix the two things that spoil most home attempts. You do not need a groundskeeper's budget. You need a mower with a rear roller.

Why stripes appear at all

A stripe is not a difference in grass colour. It is a difference in light. When grass is pressed flat in one direction, it reflects light back at you and looks pale. When it leans towards you, it looks dark. Mow one strip north, the next strip south, and your eye reads alternating light and dark bands.

The tool that does the pressing is a rear roller: a full-width cylinder behind the blade that flattens the grass as the mower passes. No roller, no stripe. A mower on four wheels will cut the grass beautifully but leave it standing more or less upright, so the light bounces back evenly and the lawn reads as one flat green.

That is the whole trick. Everything below is about doing it neatly.

What you need

  • A mower with a rear roller. This is the one non-negotiable. Front-roller and four-wheel mowers do not stripe.
  • A lawn that is dry on top. Wet grass tears and clumps, and the stripe smears.
  • Grass at mowing height, not overgrown. Stripes show best at 25mm to 40mm, cutting no more than a third of the leaf in one pass.
  • A clear edge to work to: a path, a bed, or a straight fence line to line up your first pass.

Rear-roller mowers come in petrol and cordless. For a striped finish on a medium to large lawn, self-propelled petrol is the traditional choice because the roller and the drive do the work for you. The Spectrum TG48-PRO is a self-propelled petrol mower built around a Honda engine, with a 48cm cut and a 5-year warranty. It gives you Honda reliability at a keener price than the badged Honda machines, which is why we point most stripe-seekers at it first.

Step by step: mowing the stripes

  1. Mow the perimeter first. Do one lap around the whole lawn. This gives you a turning strip at each end so you never have to reverse over a finished stripe.
  2. Set your first line straight. Pick the longest straight edge, a patio or a fence, and mow your first pass right alongside it. This first line sets every line after it, so take your time and keep it dead straight.
  3. Turn and come back the other way. At the end of the run, turn into the perimeter strip, line up next to the pass you just made, and mow back in the opposite direction. This reversal is what creates the light-then-dark contrast.
  4. Overlap by a few centimetres. Run the mower's edge slightly over the previous pass, not with a gap between them. A small overlap keeps the roller lines touching so there is no thin unstriped ribbon between bands.
  5. Finish by re-cutting the perimeter. Your first lap is now cut across by every stripe end. One final lap around the edge tidies the ends into a clean border and hides the turning marks.

Sharper stripes, and patterns

Once straight stripes feel easy, a few habits sharpen the finish.

Change direction every cut

Mow the same lines every week and the grass learns to lean one way, the stripe fades, and you can get shallow ruts from the wheels. Rotate: stripes north to south this week, east to west next week, diagonally the week after. The lawn stays healthier and the stripes stay crisp.

For a chequerboard, mow twice

Do the whole lawn in stripes one way, then mow the whole lawn again at ninety degrees. Where the two sets of bands cross you get the chequerboard effect. It takes twice as long and burns a little more fuel, but for a special weekend it is the showpiece finish.

Roll after mowing for a deeper stripe

Some gardeners go back over the finished stripes with the roller alone, engine running but blades disengaged where the mower allows, to press the bend in harder. It is optional. A good rear-roller mower stripes well enough on the cut alone.

Common mistakes

  • Expecting stripes from a four-wheel mower. The single most common disappointment. Check for a full-width rear roller before you buy if a striped lawn is the goal.
  • Cutting too short. Scalped grass has no leaf to bend, so there is nothing to catch the light. Keep it at 25mm or above in summer.
  • Mowing wet grass. The clippings clump, the roller drags them, and the stripe looks streaky. Wait for the dew to lift.
  • Wandering first line. Every stripe copies the first one. A curved first pass gives you a whole lawn of curved stripes.

The mowers that stripe best

Any true rear-roller mower will stripe. Where they differ is cut width, drive, and price.

For most lawns we recommend starting with the Spectrum TG48-PRO Honda-powered self-propelled mower: a 48cm rear-roller cut, a Honda engine, and a 5-year warranty, at a lower price than the equivalent branded machines. It is the value pick that does not compromise on the engine.

If you specifically want a Honda machine, the Honda HRH 536 QX is a 53cm rear-roller mower built for exactly this job, and the Honda HRX 476 QY covers smaller lawns. Both stripe superbly. You are paying for the badge as much as the finish, which is worth knowing before you choose.

FAQs

Do I need a special mower to stripe my lawn?

You need a mower with a rear roller. The roller flattens the grass as you mow, and that is what creates the light and dark bands. A standard four-wheel mower cuts well but will not stripe.

How do I make the stripes darker?

Let the grass grow a little longer, around 30mm to 40mm, so there is more leaf to bend and catch the light. Mowing in opposite directions and, if you wish, rolling over the finished stripes will deepen the contrast.

Why won't my stripes show up?

The usual causes are a mower with no rear roller, grass cut too short, or a lawn mown in the same direction every week. Check the mower first, then raise the cutting height, then vary your direction.

How often should I change the striping direction?

Every cut. Rotating the direction each week stops the grass leaning permanently one way, keeps the stripes sharp, and avoids wheel ruts forming in the same lines.
